# What a calibrated scanner actually measures

A scanner with shipped thresholds measures the distance between your draft and somebody's guess about a generic register. A calibrated one measures the distance between your draft and your own good writing. The difference is the whole product, and it is worth being precise about what changes when you calibrate.

## Bands, not rules

Calibration reads every sample in the human corpus, measures each one, and writes percentile bands: where the middle of your sentence lengths sits, how wide your variance runs, how often you reach for a given construction. A draft is then compared to those bands. Nothing in the catalog changes; what changes is the ruler.

The em dash is the clearest example. Its human baseline runs across a fiftyfold range, and current models sit below the mean. A gate keyed on em dashes today catches essayists, not machines, so the scanner measures it and never flags it.

My grandmother kept bees on a hillside outside Ljubljana, and every August she would sell the honey in jars that had once held pickles. The labels were her handwriting. She never wrote anything else down, as far as anyone knew.

## What the bands cannot see

Absence. A draft with no concrete detail, no defended position and a voice that never shifts scores nothing on any band, because the bands measure presence. That half needs a reader, and it is the half that usually matters more.

So calibrate, and then read. The bands tell you where you have drifted from yourself; they cannot tell you whether the piece is worth reading, and no ruler will.
